rules.statement: Take the DPoP signing key from a named, rotatable key ring shared by the application. Do not generate or store a DPoP key per session or next to the tokens it binds.
rules.why: Keeping the key apart from the tokens means stealing a session's tokens does not also give away the key that binds them, and the ring can be rotated on its own schedule.
rules.check: Look for DPoP key generation per session or user, and for DPoP private keys stored in session or token storage. Also flag a DPoP key taken from the general signing ring without its own configured name.

rules.statement: Use only asymmetric keys for DPoP proofs. Choose the algorithm from the provider's advertised `dpop_signing_alg_values_supported`, and never select a MAC algorithm or `none`.
rules.why: A DPoP proof has to be verifiable from the public JWK in its header, so symmetric keys and `none` are never valid choices.
rules.check: Look for DPoP algorithm or key selection that accepts symmetric keys, that can pick `none`, or that ignores the provider's advertised algorithm list.

rules.statement: When a token request carried a DPoP proof, require the successful response's `token_type` to be `DPoP`, compared case-insensitively. Treat any other value, such as `Bearer`, as a downgrade and reject it with an error.
rules.why: Accepting a bearer token in reply to a proof is a silent downgrade of sender-constrained tokens (RFC 9449; RFC 6749 §5.1 makes token_type case-insensitive).
rules.check: Look for token response handling after a DPoP proof that does not check `token_type`, that accepts `Bearer`, or that compares the value case-sensitively.

rules.statement: Create a fresh DPoP proof for every request. Token-endpoint proofs use `htm` POST, `htu` set to the endpoint and no `ath`. Resource-server proofs include `ath` for the access token and the cached nonce for that origin.
rules.why: RFC 9449 §4 and §7 require a unique proof per request, and require `ath` only when the proof accompanies an access token.
rules.check: Look for a proof that is cached or reused across requests, an `ath` claim on token-endpoint proofs, or resource proofs missing `ath`.

rules.statement: Retry a `use_dpop_nonce` error response at most once, and only when it carries a `DPoP-Nonce`. Build the retry with a new proof, a form rebuilt from a fresh copy of the caller's parameters, and client authentication run again, so that no client assertion is replayed.
rules.why: Replaying the same form would reuse a `private_key_jwt` assertion, and retrying without a limit could loop.
rules.check: Look for nonce retry loops, retries that resend the same form or proof, and retries that reuse an existing client assertion instead of authenticating again.

rules.statement: Store a DPoP server nonce per origin (scheme, host and port) in a size-bounded cache. Record a `DPoP-Nonce` from any response to a request that carried a proof.
rules.why: Nonces are issued per server (RFC 9449 §8), and an unbounded cache keyed by attacker-influenced origins would grow without limit.
rules.check: Look for nonce caches keyed by the full URI or kept globally, caches with no size bound, and responses whose `DPoP-Nonce` header is ignored.

rules.statement: Pin a session's DPoP key by its RFC 7638 SHA-256 JWK thumbprint (`jkt`), and sign later proofs for that session with the pinned key, even after the key ring rotates.
rules.why: Tokens are bound to `cnf.jkt`, and refresh-token binding stays continuous across rotation only if the same key keeps signing.
rules.check: Look for refresh or resource calls that pick the current or newest ring key instead of the stored `jkt`, and for thumbprints that are not RFC 7638 SHA-256.

rules.statement: When DPoP is required, detect a missing key ring, an empty ring or an unknown pinned key before sending anything, and fail with `InvalidOperationException` as a configuration error. Report a provider that advertises no usable algorithm as a provider error. Never fall back to sending the request without DPoP.
rules.why: Sending nothing when DPoP is required prevents an unbound request, and keeping configuration errors separate from provider errors makes each failure clear.
rules.check: Look for required-DPoP paths that send the request anyway, that skip DPoP silently, or that report configuration and provider failures with the same exception type.

rules.statement: Do not attach DPoP proofs to token revocation requests.
rules.why: Neither RFC 7009 nor RFC 9449 defines a DPoP proof for revocation.
rules.check: Look for DPoP proof creation or `DPoP` headers in revocation request code.

rules.statement: When the client itself writes a protocol parameter (such as `dpop_jkt`), treat its name as reserved and reject it in caller-supplied additional parameters.
rules.why: A caller-supplied copy could conflict with the client's value or override it.
rules.check: Look for new client-written request parameters that are not added to the reserved-name check for additional parameters.

rules.statement: Write the abbreviation DPoP as `DPoP` in identifiers (for example `DPoPSigningAlgValuesSupported`), not `Dpop`.
rules.why: The same casing everywhere matches the existing protocol constants and DPoP services.
rules.check: Look for new or renamed identifiers that contain `Dpop`.
